content: The World Health Organization (WHO) Pesticide Evaluation Scheme (WHOPES) was established in 1982 and operates through a four-phase evaluation and testing program to ensure the safety, efficacy, and cost-effectiveness of pesticides used for public health purposes. The program also develops and promotes policies, strategies, and guidelines for the selective and judicious application of pesticides, assisting and monitoring their implementation by member states. Phase 1 involves testing technical or formulated pesticides for efficacy and persistence using laboratory-bred arthropods. This phase also includes studying cross-resistance with existing pesticide classes and establishing diagnostic concentrations for detecting vector resistance in the field. Compounds are evaluated for their safety to humans and the environment in collaboration with WHO units and other international organizations. Additionally, WHO collaborating centers may conduct laboratory experiments to confirm toxicological and ecotoxicological data provided by manufacturers. Phase 2 focuses on small-scale field studies under controlled conditions to assess the efficacy, persistence, and appropriate application doses of pesticides on natural vector populations. This phase also examines the impact of products on non-target fauna and documents any harmful effects on operators in field settings. Phase 3 involves mediumor large-scale field trials in disease-endemic countries to evaluate the efficacy of pesticides against specific disease vectors. These trials include entomological, safety, and, where appropriate, epidemiological evaluations. WHO oversees the technical aspects of these trials, while manufacturers provide the insecticide and funding, and local institutions supply qualified staff for implementation. Phase 4 is dedicated to establishing specific technical and formulation specifications for evaluated products. Before 2002, draft specifications proposed by industry were reviewed by the WHO Expert Advisory Panel on Vector Biology and Control and issued as interim specifications. These were later reviewed every 5–6 years for potential publication as full WHO specifications. Since 2002, specifications have been developed through the Joint Meeting on Pesticide Specifications (JMPS), harmonizing procedures with the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO). WHO recommendations on use and specifications are restricted to data packages and products evaluated by WHOPES. The JMPS, established as a collaborative effort between FAO and WHO, ensures the development of joint specifications for pesticides used in both public health and agriculture. The first full meeting of the JMPS was held in 2002, and the FAO/WHO Manual was published the same year, providing guidelines for pesticide formulations, including microbial larvicides. The manual has undergone revisions to reflect scientific and technological advancements, with the most recent version available online as the current working document. FAO and WHO specifications are intended for quality assurance and risk management. The evaluation of hazards and risks associated with pesticides is based on assessments by national registration authorities or other international organizations. In the absence of such evaluations, WHO/FAO arranges detailed assessments of original studies before proceeding with specification development. The JMPS ensures that recommendations are based on informed assessments of hazards and risks. The JMPS comprises scientists with expertise in specification development, providing recommendations to FAO and WHO in their individual capacities. Industry experts may be invited to provide additional information or technical expertise. The primary function of the JMPS is to recommend the adoption, extension, modification, or withdrawal of specifications. Test methods cited in FAO/WHO specifications are validated through inter-laboratory trials conducted by organizations such as the Collaborative International Pesticides Analytical Council (CIPAC) and AOAC International. These methods include peer-validated analytical techniques for relevant impurities and physical-chemical properties of pesticide formulations.
